data.title: Dermatofibroma — viva
data.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 10 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Dermatofibroma** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. Write short notes on dermatofibroma (PYQ).**
- Common benign fibrohistiocytic tumour (benign fibrous histiocytoma) — firm, button-like, slightly raised, pink-brown papule/nodule usually on legs of young women; often after minor trauma (insect bite, folliculitis, shaving) — reactive vs clonal debated
- Dimple (Fitzpatrick) sign: lateral compression produces central dimpling because the lesion is tethered to the overlying epidermis

**Q2. Dermoscopy.**
- Central white scar-like patch with delicate peripheral pigment network (light-brown); dotted vessels; ring-like globules

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Ill-defined dermal proliferation of spindle fibroblasts and histiocytes (foam cells, haemosiderin-laden siderophages, Touton giant cells) with collagen trapping at the periphery ('collagen balls'), sparing of a grenz zone
- Overlying epidermis hyperplastic with flat-bottomed elongated pigmented rete ridges ('dirty fingers') and induction of follicular/sebaceous structures (basaloid induction mimicking BCC)
- Factor XIIIa positive, CD34 negative (vs DFSP: CD34 positive, factor XIIIa negative)

**Q4. Variants.**
- Aneurysmal (haemosiderotic — rapid growth, bluish), cellular (higher recurrence), atypical (pseudosarcomatous), epithelioid, lipidised (ankle), multiple eruptive dermatofibromas (SLE, HIV, immunosuppression)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP — larger, growing, multinodular plaque on trunk, CD34+, COL1A1–PDGFB fusion; treat with Mohs/wide excision, imatinib for advanced)
- Melanocytic naevus, melanoma (pigmented DF), keloid/hypertrophic scar, BCC, Kaposi sarcoma, prurigo nodule, epidermoid cyst, Spitz naevus, xanthoma

**Q6. Enumerate painful skin tumours (PYQ).**
- Mnemonic BLENDAN-GG: Blue rubber bleb naevus, Leiomyoma, Eccrine spiradenoma, Neuroma, Dermatofibroma (sometimes), Angiolipoma, Neurilemmoma (schwannoma), Glomus tumour, Granular cell tumour; also chondrodermatitis nodularis helicis, keloid, endometrioma, calcinosis cutis, MPNST

**Q7. Management.**
- Reassurance — benign, often persists; excision if symptomatic, enlarging, cosmetically troublesome or diagnostic doubt (scar may be worse than lesion)
- Cryotherapy, intralesional steroids, lasers (flatten/lighten) — partial results

**Q8. Is dermatofibroma a reactive lesion or a neoplasm?**
- Debated — traditionally a reactive fibrohistiocytic proliferation after minor trauma (insect bite, folliculitis, shaving), but clonality (PRKCB/PRKCD gene fusions) suggests a benign neoplasm; multiple eruptive dermatofibromas occur in SLE, HIV, immunosuppression, pregnancy

**Q9. What is the dimple (Fitzpatrick) sign?**
- Lateral compression of the lesion causes it to dimple downward (central depression) because of tethering to the overlying epidermis — characteristic of dermatofibroma

**Q10. Differentiate dermatofibroma from dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP).**
- DFSP: larger, enlarging, multinodular indurated plaque on trunk, slow but locally aggressive; CD34+ (DF is CD34−, factor XIIIa+); storiform spindle cells infiltrating fat in honeycomb pattern; t(17;22) COL1A1–PDGFB fusion; treat with Mohs surgery, imatinib for unresectable

## Quick spotter facts
- Firm leg papule with positive dimple sign — dermatofibroma
- Factor XIIIa+ / CD34− (DFSP is CD34+)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Fibrohistiocytic tumours). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
